newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Poll finds Americans don't understand HK people.
newsitem.headline: Poll finds Americans don't understand HK people.

text.p: Americans just don't get it when it comes to Hong Kong, new polls prepared for the Asia Society of New York found.

Two new parallel polls designed to compare U.S. attitudes with those of Hong Kong residents showed a large gap between the perceptions of Americans about the transition and Hong Kong residents' feelings about the handover, the Asia Society said on Thursday.
"Americans have largely negative feelings about the changes taking place in Hong Kong and mistakenly believe that Hong Kong residents do also," the Asia Society said in a release.

"Indeed, a large majority of Hong Kong residents feel that things are moving in the right direction and think things will get better, while Americans hold a much more pessimistic view," the society said.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
The two telephone polls, which were conducted by Wirthlin Worldwide, surveyed 1,000 people in Hong Kong and 1,000 people in the United States.
Both polls were taken last week.
The Hong Kong poll found that 42 percent of Hong Kong people feel that the territory's future will be brighter after July 1 and 37 percent feel that it will be the same.
Only 16 percent said they believed the future will be worse.
In contrast, 73 percent of Americans said they expected Hong Kong's prospects to be worse after the transfer.
The poll also found that Hong Kong people are much less concerned about personal freedoms than Americans.

Whereas 48 percent of Americans surveyed said they were very or slightly worried about personal freedoms in Hong Kong after the handover, only 18 percent of Hong Kong residents expressed concern over this issue.
The results showed that most Americans did not believe that Hong Kong people approved of the Provisional Legislature, the body installed by Beijing to replace the elected council.
Less than a quarter of Americans who said they were aware of the transition believed that the people of Hong Kong approve of the Provisional Legislature.
In reality, 62 percent of Hong Kong people believe that the Provisional Legislature can function as a legitimate legislative body until elections can be held.
Fifty-seven percent of Americans surveyed also believed that, given the choice, Hong Kong people would prefer to be independent of both Britain and China.
But only 27 percent of Hong Kong people yearned for complete independence, while 46 percent said they wanted to join China.
